The lesson as written is still refuted, for four reasons. (1) VALUE: it has zero effect on the private score. It is a post-deadline process note, not a mechanism. (2) The retro-test does not need to wait for the deadline. It can be run today from CONTEXT, and its core hypothesis ('most breaks follow a surprising read') already fails. Stop/ban clauses broken or reopened 23-27 Sep: (a) 23 Sep, the 8 Sep 'post-proc probes closed' rule was lifted by the user under a target (l.1162); (b) 26 Sep 20:33Z, the R7/R9 public-ladder ban was lifted by the user (l.2389); (c) 21:21Z, the session read R8 as lifted for the retrain (l.2454/2508; suspended at 01:31Z); (d) 05:28Z, the 43/44 deviation, the ONLY one triggered by a surprising read (dc0.30 -0.005); (e) 11:08Z, E10 v3 lifted R8 and the P6 ban (user); (f) 11:09Z, 'class C never a final' was reopened by user letter (b), downstream of (d); (g) 11:11Z, 'no retraining before 29 Sep' was reopened and exp71 pushed (user yes); (h) 11:14Z, the round-15 FREEZE was lifted by the user out of rank dissatisfaction, and new division-side rungs exp70g/exp70n followed (l.2940-2945). That is 1 surprise-triggered break of 8 (2 of 8 if (f) counts). The dominant trigger is leaderboard-rank pressure coming through the user, not surprising reads. So 'pre-declare the surprise branch' is a generalisation from one case, and the I-338 entry it would add targets the wrong failure mode. (3) The claim that the FREEZE 'saved honesty' no longer holds: the user lifted the freeze about 5 h later (11:14Z). s3.12 must record that or it overstates the safeguard. (4) As designed, the test is not a real test. The author wrote the expected answer in advance, 'surprising' has no operational definition, n is under 10, and it is scored in hindsight by the same session. FEASIBILITY is trivial (text only, 0 GPU, no kernel, no R1-R10 contact, byte-identity n/a), so the only problem is validity, not schedule.
